subject: religious-studies

moments.title: Guru Nanak is born
moments.who: Nanak, in Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan)
moments.body: Born on 15 April 1469 (some traditions place it on the full moon of Kartik in October-November). He grew up in Mughal-era Punjab amid Hindu-Muslim tensions, working as an accountant before his spiritual experience around 1499.
moments.takeaway: Sikh tradition emphasises Nanak's distinctness from both Hindu and Muslim traditions of his time. He is said to have responded to his vision with 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.'

moments.title: Ten human Gurus
moments.body: The ten human Gurus: Nanak (1469-1539), Angad (1539-1552), Amar Das (1552-1574), Ram Das (1574-1581), Arjan (1581-1606, martyred by Mughals), Hargobind (1606-1644), Har Rai (1644-1661), Har Krishan (1661-1664), Tegh Bahadur (1664-1675, martyred), Gobind Singh (1675-1708).
moments.takeaway: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604. The 'martial' tradition emerged under Hargobind in response to Mughal persecution.

moments.title: Founding of the Khalsa
moments.body: Vaisakhi (April) 1699: Guru Gobind Singh asks for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) step forward. They are initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword) and then themselves initiate the Guru. The Khalsa — community of the 'pure' — is founded.
moments.takeaway: The Khalsa is marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan). Members take the surnames Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women, symbolically equalising caste and gender.

moments.title: Guru Granth Sahib as eternal Guru
moments.who: Guru Gobind Singh before his death
moments.body: Before his death (from an Afghan assassin's wound), Guru Gobind Singh declares the Guru Granth Sahib — the scripture compiled by Guru Arjan with additions — to be the eternal Guru. There will be no more human Gurus.
moments.takeaway: Scripture as Guru ended succession disputes. The Guru Granth Sahib is treated as a living Guru, bowed to, awakened in the morning and put to rest at night.

now.title: Sikhism today
now.body:
Sikhism has around 25-30 million adherents, mostly in Punjab (India) and the Sikh diaspora (UK, Canada, US). The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) at Amritsar (built under Guru Arjan) is the central shrine. Daily langar (free communal meal) at the Golden Temple serves around 100,000 people.

Major 20th-century events: Partition (1947) split Punjab and displaced millions; Operation Blue Star (1984) by the Indian army at the Golden Temple, and the assassination of Indira Gandhi by her Sikh bodyguards months later, traumatised the community.
now.open_questions: How should Sikhism relate to Hinduism and Islam? Some scholars frame it as a syncretic movement of medieval Punjab; Sikhs themselves emphasise its distinctness from the start.

reflection: Sikhism is the youngest of the major world religions with a clear founder. Its trajectory from Nanak's spiritual vision (1499) to the founding of the Khalsa (1699) to the eternal Guru Granth Sahib (1708) is dense and well-documented — a religion whose origins are not obscured by myth.
